Calculus II with Prof. Haddad was a mid-program core that I took mainly because it was required, and I had enough time, though my motivation fluctuated and deadlines piled up on me unexpectedly. The LMS and submission flow stayed smooth, which helped when I was juggling other courses, but I still found the lectures serviceable rather than memorable, while peer discussion often saved me more than the official slides did. I remember one early moment of confusion around improper integrals that shaped how I approached the rest of the term, and I appreciated the detailed feedback, even if the grading comments came slower than I wanted. I’d only recommend it if you’re prepared for a grind and have a plan for staying motivated.

I went into Linear Algebra kind of rusty and left feeling mixed, but I have to admit Dr. Miller knows how to push you when you’re not keeping up. The math itself felt doable on a good day, but the pacing was uneven—some weeks I felt a bit behind and then sprinted to catch up as deadlines loomed, which made the whole thing feel more stressful than it should have been. The materials were a sore spot for me; the problem sets and notes didn’t click the way I’d hoped, and I ended up relying on a few scattered lecture clips more than a coherent text, which left gaps I could feel when I tried to apply concepts later. I appreciated the quick feedback on submissions, but the explanations were thin, like “this is wrong, try again,” with not enough walk-throughs to really illuminate the thought process. I do like that the difficulty kept me honest, and I gave myself a partial pass even though I still ended up in the failed range, because the struggle had its own sting of learning. A concrete memory—one late-night project where I finally connected eigenvectors to a practical stability problem—felt almost earned, but the administrative friction around tooling setup kept stealing time before I could get there.

I kept up with nearly every lecture in Data Structures this summer, and the pace was brutal enough that I often felt like I was sprinting through concepts that needed more time to click. Dr. Park explains the ideas conceptually in a way that makes sense in the moment, but the examples are thin and I kept wishing for a concrete demo I could cling to, especially when the data structures started overlapping in complicated ways. The platform quirks were a drain—some registration quirks and a confusing submission UI that could make a simple reminder feel like a small crisis—so I dreaded the small, last-minute nudges about deadlines. I remember an early confusion about Big-O for nested loops that lingered and colored the rest of the term, and oddly that misstep shaped how I approached later material, even as the assessments felt fair but exhausting. The grading comments were detailed but arrived much later than I’d hoped, which left me stuck for explanations when I was trying to study for the next thing while juggling other demanding courses. Overall, it felt like a solid foundation you could build on if you survive the pace, but the prerequisites seemed to expect more prior knowledge than advertised.

I’m a returning student who felt rusty, and I took Data Structures mainly because I heard it’s useful for industry work; Prof. Cohen’s lectures were clear and the pacing decent, but I used the materials only when needed, and the project-heavy setup with high-stakes exams kept me cautious.

I’m a returning student who feels a bit rusty, and Linear Algebra sits squarely in the middle of a heavy semester, so I came in expecting to scratch out some understanding and maybe salvage a few skills. The tooling, especially the software stack we use for homework, starts rough—every assignment seemed to ping at some missing package or outdated notebook—yet it settles into something manageable as the weeks drag on, which was a small win I clung to. Quick feedback helps a little: I’d get the grading notes back in time to adjust the next problem set, but I still felt a gap whenever a concept clicked only after a peer discussion or a side chat with a TA. The course feels like it benefits most if you already know the adjacent material, and I’m not sure how well it would land for someone entirely new in the middle of a heavy term. We do one project with matrices and a random deadline pattern that caught me off guard, and honestly the official materials didn’t lock in the intuition as cleanly as a few half-hour chat sessions with peers did, which left me feeling mixed—like I learned a lot but disliked the experience sometimes. Overall, I’d say it’s decent if you hunt with friends and don’t mind wrestling with the rough edges.

Operating Systems was a solid fit for my last semester when I needed a schedule-friendly, required track course. The lectures were clear, deadlines were frequent but manageable, and the tooling felt smooth, though email support lagged when deadlines loomed.

Linear Algebra felt like a refreshing break from the chaos of fall, but as mid-semester wore on I found my attendance slipping while juggling two other heavy courses. The pacing was fine enough in class, and the grading comments were detailed when they finally showed up, just not promptly, which left me guessing on several problem sets. I came in thinking it would be useful for industry work, and some parts clicked, but the report-heavy workload and late feedback ate into study time I needed for other deadlines. I noticed students helping each other more than staff, and communication from admins could be sloppy at times, though policies were reasonable. Overall, I’d still recommend it to peers, though be ready for delayed notes and a few busy weeks.

I started out pretty engaged, but the summer sprint and juggling a full-time job wore it down fast, especially with the tooling glitches that killed a lot of deadline weeks; still, the math builds on the prereqs, and the feedback, though delayed, was pretty detailed when it finally came.

Calculus II with Dr. Park started off with the expectation that it would be useful for industry work, and I did find some value in how the chain rule and series tests show up in later projects. The pacing felt positive overall, especially once we got past the first two units and the exams finally lined up with the practice problems I had in mind, even though deadlines stacked up unexpectedly. I’m comfortable with proofs but not heavy systems work, so some of the recurrence relations still felt abstract until the midterm project click happened. Feedback was sparse until it was basically too late to adjust, and emailing the support when deadlines pressed never felt timely. Memory anchors this around a late-semester turning point when I realized I’d be stuck without a bit more guidance.

Took Calculus II while working full-time, and the pacing felt brutal around mid-semester; the platform quirks and unclear group expectations didn’t help. Prof. Rios’s detailed comments finally came, but they’d show up after a long delay, leaving me guessing what mattered most.

I took Database Systems mainly to fit my schedule, not out of passion, and the course built nicely on the stated prerequisites, though I’m not sure the final grade reflected my understanding; peer discussions helped more than the official materials, and deadlines were rough.

I took Machine Learning mostly because it’s required for my degree, and I’ve been trying to fit study around short evening sessions during a heavy semester, so I leaned heavily on the recordings and notes. The admin side was a pain to set up at first, with the tooling frictions sticking out more than I expected, even though the LMS and submission flow itself ends up smooth enough once you’re in. The collaboration expectations felt unclear, and I’m still not sure what counts as “good” participation, which clashes with how I juggle a lot of other tasks. A few surprises linger: I think this works best if you already know some adjacent material, and honestly I’d only recommend it if you come in prepared for that turning point near the end that shifts how you see the whole thing.

man, i’m basically new to this whole ML thing and this mid-semester slog is… a lot. the tooling felt rough at first, and the first few notebooks were a battle, but it got smoother as i clung to peer discussions more than the official slides. the deadlines hit kind of hard, and email support was slow, but the hands-on project (a small classifier) finally clicked after i talked through it with a classmate who explained it like “practice makes imperfect but useful.”

Took Linear Algebra this summer under Dr. Miller while juggling a full-time job, so the pacing felt compressed but the LMS flow kept submissions smooth. The heavy report load wore me out, and a few weeks stretched into exhausting weeks with little peer dependency.

Operating Systems was solid but rough around the edges: I had a strong coding background and weak theory, so I leaned on the recordings and notes more than live lectures. The software stack started clunky, but by midterm I could push through projects, though the grading comments came late and felt detailed yet slow to reflect changes, which left me juggling deadlines. My one standout memory: an early confusion about process scheduling that colored the rest of the term and made office hours feel like a rescue.

Data Structures was okay to get the specialization credit, but the organization felt scrambled and deadlines piled up, making it hard to keep up. I mostly relied on recordings and notes, the slides were serviceable but not memorable, and the grade came after a curve.

Calculus II clarified a lot of the big ideas for me, especially the conceptual stuff, but the examples felt sparse and left me puzzled at times. The lectures were clear, and the LMS flow was smooth, yet I relied mostly on recordings and notes because motivation waxed and waned; deadlines stacked up in a way that made it hard to stay consistent. I’d still recommend it to others who are genuinely curious, even if you end up piecing things together on your own sometimes.

I ended up with a mixed feel about Database Systems, especially since I was juggling a full-time job last semester. I learned a lot, even if the process dragged on and the experience wasn’t smooth. The weekly tooling hiccups and the long, report-heavy deadlines made the weeks feel chaotic, and some days the instructions left too much room for interpretation. I remember looping in with Prof. Cohen during one late office hours—soothing to get a concrete pointer on a tricky data model question, but the feedback on assignments varied a lot, sometimes helpful, sometimes oddly vague. Overall, I feel more capable, but the journey was rough and I’m glad it’s over.

Linear Algebra was a decent fit for my curiosity, especially in the middle of a brutal semester, but I walked away with a few nagging gaps. The lecturer’s explanations felt a step behind the pace, and I kept wondering if the prerequisite talk about eigenvectors and subspaces actually lined up with what we were tested on; it sometimes seemed assumed rather than taught. I did appreciate that the LMS flow was smooth and that feedback came quick enough to adjust, though the rubric for grading felt vague enough to leave me second-guessing what counted, which didn’t help during a week with multiple deadlines. I remember one week where the midterm felt oddly heavy and I clung to office hours and the TA’s quick clarifications to stay afloat, even as I fell behind then caught up right before the next deadline.

I took Database Systems in my first semester because it was basically a degree requirement, and I did manage to catch up after falling behind around the midterm deadlines, which felt like a small victory given I was juggling full-time work. Prof. Cohen is solid enough, and the prerequisite gaps I had actually turned out to be addressed better than I expected, so that part felt smoother than I feared. The course is mostly individual work, with not much peer dependency, and people tended to help each other more than the staff did, which was sometimes enough to keep me moving when I hit a snag. There aren’t a ton of assessments, but each one matters a lot, so I was always feeling the pressure to get it right on the next submission, which kept the pace uneven. The materials were fine in a neutral way, and the accessibility of content was similarly neutral, no glaring gaps or obvious weak points. A late-semester turning point—finishing the final project with a deadline cluster—felt like the moment I finally stabilized my routine, even if I still hesitated about some of the design choices. Overall, it fits as a practical stepping stone rather than something I’d gush about.

Database Systems was worth my curiosity, but the vibe was mixed: the lectures felt useful only as a reference and the recording dragged on dryly, while the admin notes left a lot up to interpretation, which didn’t help when I was lukewarm on motivation. The TAs were quick to reply and practical, and I get that the material fits best if you already know related topics, but I still ended up failing and unsure if I’d take it again—only with solid prep first. One concrete snag: the midterm had a weird open-ended section that rewarded buzzword accuracy more than applied thinking.

Data Structures felt like a slog during a heavy midsemester, especially since juggling a full-time job made the tooling setup feel longer than the payoff. Prof. Rios retrieved decent slides, but the grading comments dragged late and the admin friction in tool setup left me frustrated.

Calculus II dragged on midterm week; my strong coding background made the theory feel thin, and the few assessments mattered a lot, so I barely passed while juggling the platform quirks and late-night deadline quirks, but Prof. Alvarez’s office hours saved me.

I’m new to this discipline and learning the basics, and Data Structures felt like a required hurdle more than a doorway to real understanding. The assessments are exhausting and feel predictably overbearing for someone still grappling with the basics; even when I think I’ve nailed a concept, the next assignment spotlights tiny edge cases and drags the energy out of me. The course pretends to be about relevance to real coding, but the problems often read like abstract puzzles that don’t map clearly to what I’ll actually do in a specialization, which left me wondering why some topics were foregrounded while others seemed buried. Group work can add value when you get a solid team, yet I watched a few peers carry the load while I scrambled to keep up, which didn’t help my confidence. Feedback is sparse until it’s almost too late, and the email support drags on during deadlines, so the moment I needed guidance most I just got a slow pushback. There was one practical project—the tiny hash-table with separate chaining—that felt doable and tangible, but the overall design of the assessments still wore me out and left me feeling like I had to push through more than learn.

Taking Machine Learning as a mid-program core while juggling several demanding courses was rough but doable, and Prof. Alvarez’s class gradually felt like it clicked around week 8 or so. The ramp from accessible concepts to sharper topics was real—the early assignments helped, but the later projects and the heavy exam component hit hard, especially with the time pressure staying just about manageable most weeks. Office hours saved me more than once when a misread data split turned a project error into an anxious afternoon, and the quick feedback helped adjust approaches fast enough to keep the next deadline from spiraling. One concrete memory: the final project required a small neural net on a Kaggle-ish dataset, which was enlightening yet made me question whether the grading was more about the idea or the execution. Overall, I felt rusty at first, then steadily pushed to catch up.

Operating Systems was the main focus for the term, and with a full-time job I barely had time to breathe, let alone keep up with the uneven week-to-week teaching. The few assessments felt heavy, and I barely scraped through after a mid‑semester crunch, partly because the feedback from the professor was inconsistent and the communication about deadlines felt sloppy. Peer discussion helped a lot more than the official materials, so I leaned on my lab group to sanity-check what we were supposed to internalize for the big exam week—one memorable moment where the week of code review and a tricky page table question finally clicked, but it was closer to the deadline than ideal. Overall, it was a mid-program core course that wore me down and left me wishing for a bit more clarity and steadiness.

I’m a returning student who felt rusty, and Machine Learning dragged along in the middle of a brutal semester. Grading felt unclear, and I barely passed after struggling most of the term.

The forums helped me when I hit the tough bits, though sometimes the replies sounded dismissive, which didn’t help my confidence. A late-semester moment—nailing a tricky binary search tree question in the last week—felt like a small personal win amid the chaos.

I took Database Systems while working full-time, and the workload was surprisingly manageable in bursts, especially when I could carve out a study group and knock out a set of problems together. I liked the instructor well enough, but the grading felt uneven and I never quite trusted whether my C would reflect what I actually understood, which left me unsure mid-term. Attendance started engaged, then faded as the weeks got busier, and I remember one early confusion about normalization that shaped how I approached the rest of the term. The forums helped, though sometimes they sounded dismissive, and the course works best if you have peers to hash things out with; otherwise the material felt too fragmented week to week.

Midway through the term, Prof. Haddad’s lectures are clear and pace fine, but the materials feel thin for someone juggling a full-time job and limited study time. I appreciated the office hours and TA tips, yet the grading rubric remains vague and the deadlines stack up unexpectedly; a single confusing point early on in Linear Algebra still lingers for me.

I took Calculus II in the summer term while working full-time, so I appreciated the toolset being fairly usable even with my limited study time. The project-heavy pace plus some high-stakes exams meant I relied a lot on the group work and the few times the team functioned well, we caught each other up on the shared notes and weekly problem sets. The grading rubric felt vague at times, which didn’t help when I tried to gauge what counted toward the final B I earned—exhausting, but fair enough for the effort I could put in. It sometimes felt like students helped each other more than staff did, and the occasional reminder about deadlines was enough to keep me on track, even as tightening pacing wore me down.

I took Data Structures mainly because it was a degree requirement, and my strong coding background didn’t quite translate to the theory here. The lectures’ slides are serviceable but not memorable, and I found the forums okay most of the time yet occasionally dismissive when I asked about a basic concept. Group work helped when the teammates showed up and stayed on task, but I felt the assessment was fair enough even though it wore me out—time pressure was usually manageable, and the project deadline pattern was a bit sneaky

Taking Cyber Security Basics mid-program while juggling a full-time job was chaotic in a good way: the conceptual explanations landed, but I relied on the office hours to untangle a stubborn module about threat modeling. The course moves fast with lots of deadlines, and I found the assignment-heavy rhythm pushed me to keep up, though I used the materials selectively when needed. I learned a ton, especially compared to another term’s more hands-on course, but I still can’t shake the feeling I disliked the grind of always chasing the next due date. I’d say the best surprise was how much a study group helped me keep pace, even if the examples in lectures stayed a bit thin. The turning point came late in the semester when a stray lab file finally clicked, and I felt genuinely energized to finish strong.

This course was… useful in bits, but the pacing felt off for someone juggling a full-time job. Grading feedback comes only after delays, and the mismatch between lectures and assessments bugged me more than once, especially compared to the easier prerequisite I took before.

I’m in my last semester and took Database Systems mostly out of genuine curiosity about how data really flows, not just because it’s required, and I’m glad I did. Prof. Alvarez is thoughtful, but the lectures feel dry as recordings—still, I nerded out listening to the way he explains normalization until it finally clicked, even if I had to replay sections. The mix of a heavy project load and high-stakes exams kept my schedule honest, and I liked how the project demanded real design choices rather than just theory, though the feedback often showed up too late to adjust the current draft. Some assignments varied a lot in how helpful the feedback was, which was frustrating when a concrete grading quirk would pop up right before the deadline, like a necessary schema choice that wasn’t clearly specified in the prompt. The course lands solidly on the practical side, with tools and concepts that feel usable, but the timing and consistency of comments could be jittery, and that purple patch of late feedback during a busy period was hard to absorb. Overall, the project-heavy setup suits the topic, even as I wish the feedback timing were more predictable.

I took Operating Systems as a required course for my track, and I was juggling it with another hard class, so I fell behind for a while and then scrambled to catch up around the deadlines. The practical parts were where I felt I learned something useful, like when we did the small project on process synchronization—seeing how wakeups and signals actually play out helped me understand why some things in the notes clicked only after I tried to implement them. But the vibe in the class was messy: the collaboration expectations felt unclear, and I wasn’t sure who was supposed to do what in group work, which didn’t help when I was trying to stay on top of it. Grading comments arrived later than I’d hoped, and by the time I got feedback it didn’t always help me fix the specific issues I’d run into while coding or studying for the next thing. The prerequisite material felt helpful only if you already know adjacent material, so I survived by skating along on what I knew and hoping for the best. Overall, I learned a lot, but the experience left me frustrated and unsure whether I’d recommend it.

Machine Learning was a required checkpoint in my first semester, and I went into it juggling a full-time job, which meant I started off engaged but attendance faded as midterms and work nights piled up. The lectures did a solid job breaking down concepts at a high level, but the real gaps showed up in the examples—there weren't enough concrete, real-world demos to map the ideas to my data, so I often left after the key terms without a clear sense of how to apply them. The staff answered questions in the help forum, sure, but most of the back-and-forth helper energy came from classmates, which was fine until a few tricky topics needed quick validation. The course did a better job than I expected at filling prerequisite gaps, and I appreciated the focus on theory enough to keep slogging through assignments that felt heavy and deadline-driven week after week. A standout quirk: the weekly problem sets were heavy on coding practice but the feedback sometimes came late, so I learned to pace myself around the deadlines, especially around the project submission window. Compared to another course from the same term, this one leaned more on conceptual explanations, but the thinness of applied examples kept it from clicking as smoothly as I hoped. Overall, it was messy and doable, with one dominant snag that stuck with me.

I’m new to linear algebra and stuck with a rough start: I remember the first week’s confusion about vectors that colored the rest of the term, even though the lectures were clear and paced fine. The admin side really dragged—feedback arrived too late to help before deadlines, and the software stack started rough but got manageable after a while. I barely passed, fell behind and caught up around deadlines, and the grading didn’t feel aligned with the effort I put in. Still, I liked the instructor and the overall vibe, just not the timing of reviews or the rough patches in the platform.

Came into Computer Networks because it’s required, and Dr. Park’s lectures felt uneven week to week. The platform quirks stressed me out, but the office hours rescued me—especially during the week with the big router assignment, which still felt exhausting even though the final was fair.

Cyber Security Basics in my first semester felt useful in bits, but the load dragged on because the report-heavy tasks stacked up and the feedback varied a lot by assignment. The conceptual explanations clicked, yet the concrete examples were thin, and platform quirks added extra stress (like weird submission quirks right before a deadline). I’ll admit I learned something, but I can’t say I’d recommend it despite the bit of value it offered.

In my first semester, Data Structures with Prof. Cohen felt uneven week to week, and the instructions left too much room for interpretation; peer discussions saved me more than the official materials, especially when juggling another demanding course, though the grading comments came late.

I took Operating Systems with Dr. Park while juggling a full-time job, and I found it more useful for industry work than I expected, but the steady grind and deadlines got me behind at times. The grading rubric felt vague and slow to explain, and responses from email support when deadlines loomed were not timely, which didn’t help. I used the forums and office hours to catch up, and the course helped fill some prerequisite gaps, but it wasn’t enjoyable and I wouldn’t necessarily recommend it.

I took Computer Networks mostly because it was a degree requirement, and I felt I could keep up if I treated it like a project clock rather than a class. Dr. Park is clearly thoughtful and I liked his explanations, even when I ended up disagreeing with the grading approach he used for some quizzes—the rubric felt surprisingly opaque, but the actual marking was transparent enough to see where I went wrong after the next deadline. The LMS flow worked well, submissions were straightforward, and the week-by-week deadlines helped me juggle full-time work, though I did fall behind a bit and then sprinted to catch up right before the midterm window. I found the course benefits from study group vibes—when a few of us compared notes, gaps in the prerequisite material surfaced faster than I expected, and the group picked up the pace together. In practice, the support from peers was stronger than staff guidance, which was a mixed bag but kept me moving. I’m left with a sense that the course fills the prerequisite holes better than I anticipated, even if I’d trade a bit of the grading ambiguity for a clearer signal on how my score actually reflects my understanding. Overall, I did learn a fair bit, but the arithmetic of the grade still rubbed me the wrong way.

I’m new to this stuff and kept up with nearly every lecture, but I left the term barely passing because the lecturer’s explanations felt scattered and hard to connect to the basics I was still trying to grasp. The course felt like an advanced elective that assumed more prior knowledge than advertised, and the tool setup took ages for a payoff that didn’t always land in class. The workload wasn’t brutal each week, and I managed most weeks despite the time pressure, but the assessment mix didn’t line up with what we actually covered in lectures. In practice, classmates tended to help each other more than the staff did, which helped more than any official guidance, and I’ll remember the week of the big router-simulation exam more than anything else. I’m not sure I’d recommend it to someone new to the discipline.

The first semester in the program with Prof. Cohen was a mixed bag: I kept up with nearly every lecture, but the way the course leaned on a few high-stakes assessments made every small thing feel heavier than it should. The conceptual explanations were strong, but the examples we actually got to work through felt thin, so I spent extra time trying to map everything to real OS issues on my own after class while juggling a full-time job. The platform quirks and some grading rubric vagueness added needless stress—typos in the assignment portal and unclear expectations for how a design question would be scored made the few due dates feel like moving targets. I remember the late-semester turning point when a tricky exam question finally clicked after a long night of cross-checking notes; that moment shifted my view, even though I wouldn’t want to repeat the setup. There was one project where a small misalignment between the rubric and the rubric’s emphasis on depth hurt my grade more than the actual work did, and I left wishing the assessment profile offered a bit more bite across multiple tasks. Still, the course did push me toward understanding enough to feel capable for the next phase, even if I’d approach it differently next time.

Took Cyber Security Basics while juggling a full-time job, so the pace felt heavy but doable. The stack started rough, a bit of head-scratching, then more manageable as weeks passed. Instructions sometimes left too much room for interpretation, and the forums could be helpful yet occasionally dismissive, which wore me down during the tougher weeks, like that midterm week I barely slept.

I’m glad I took Database Systems as an advanced elective with Dr. Chen, but I’m basically exhausted and still unsure if the grade reflected what I actually understood. I started out engaged, but by mid-semester my attendance faded as the weekly report-heavy workload piled up and I started to feel like I was chasing deadlines more than mastering concepts. The platform quirks didn’t help—erratic submission confirmations and a few times I forgot where to attach a long data-models document, which just added stress on top of the already tight schedule. One concrete moment sticks: a midterm where a seemingly straightforward schema normalization question turned into a time-sink because the tool’s UI misled me about where to export the result, which left me scrambling to fix it right before class. I appreciated that the course filled some gaps in prerequisites better than I expected, but that early confusion about functional dependencies still colored how I approached later topics. Overall I feel tired and resigned, juggling this with another hard class, and I’m not confident the grade truly maps my understanding, even though the peer discussions with classmates were genuinely helpful.

Midway through this heavy semester, I’m honestly not sure I’d recommend Calculus II, at least not without serious caveats. Dr. Park seems fine in person, but the overall flow of the course has felt disorganized, with announcements and policy details pinging around in a way that makes it hard to track what actually matters for the next quiz. The lectures themselves hit the main ideas, yet the prerequisites assume more prior exposure than advertised, so I’m constantly scrambling to connect the dots between the old limits stuff and the new integration techniques. I study in short evening blocks, and I’ve found that when I finally sit down to go through a problem set, the feedback is thorough but often late, which irks me because I’m trying to adjust before the next test. It also seems like the help channel is more effective when students warn each other about tricky parts than when staff chimes in, which is fine but feels off for a class that sells itself as supported. One concrete memory sticks: the weekly project on polar coordinates, where the deadline sneaks up after a long set of lectures, and the forum thread with a clarifying example from a fellow student helped more than the official office-hours moment I visited, which was crowded and not as productive as I’d hoped.

I took the Machine Learning course mainly out of genuine curiosity, but the whole thing felt off-kilter from the start in a summer term with that brutal compressed pace. The material starts accessible and then ramps up sharply, which hit my nerves because I’ve got a solid coding background but weak theory, so I spent more time chasing intuition than building practical intuition, if that makes sense. The collaboration part was murky—clear what you’re supposed to do, not clear how to actually coordinate, so I pairs-up only when forced and still felt like we were shooting in the dark. Deadlines came in a pattern that wasn’t clean: quick feedback that let me adjust, but the back-and-forth with the TA on project specifics felt flaky and frustrating. By midterm I compared it to another course from the same term and realized this one doesn’t stack up in clarity or pacing, even though a tiny project on a classifier helped me see something nontrivial. I wouldn’t take it again, even though it did push me to poke at gaps in my theory, and I’m left with a sense that the admin side could be calmer and the expectations more concrete.

I signed up for the Machine Learning course to plug into a specialization, and I’m glad I could catch up around the deadlines, even though the setup and the instructions felt a bit open to interpretation. The peer discussions helped more than the official materials, and office hours were my rescue for tricky parts, but the tool setup and platform quirks ate into learning payoff. I learned a lot, but the experience left me mixed and not sure whether I’d recommend it.

I signed up for Operating Systems mostly because it fit my odd evening schedule and I figured I could squeeze it around my full-time job, even though I’m not super into the theory itself. The lectures were strong at explaining concepts, but the real-world examples felt sparse, so I kept trying to map threads and scheduling onto something tangible, which didn’t always land. Group work helped when the team actually functioned, but when it devolved into someone dominating or someone vanishing, the whole thing slowed to a crawl and my motivation tanked. The prerequisites start accessible and then spike quickly into things that felt out of reach after a long day; I managed by skinning through every week’s reading but I still felt the edges wobble during labs. Feedback often arrived too late to fix the next deadline, which was frustrating in a course that demands timely iteration, and I wound up juggling the grading quirks and a late project patch while trying to keep my job from collapsing around me. I learned a lot, but I can’t honestly say I’d recommend it; the overall experience was rough enough that the value didn’t quite outweigh the grind.

Calculus II with Dr. Park was required for my degree, and I took it over the summer term while juggling a full-time job, so the compressed pacing hit me hard. The tooling and online platform gave me a few headaches during deadline weeks, which made those modules feel twice as long as they were supposed to be, especially when a quiz window would stumble or a graphing calculator feature would stall mid-work. Dr. Park’s teaching felt uneven week to week, and some lectures clicked while others felt like a slog, so I leaned on office hours to piece things together—those sessions were a genuine lifeline and totally rescued the course for me when the material started masking itself in the notation. The feedback sometimes arrived too late to help with the next problem set, which stung given the time crunch, and I kept a small checklist of things to review before exams just to stay sane. One concrete win was a midterm format that mixed short proofs with a couple of applied problems, which kept me honest about what I actually needed to practice. I’d recommend it only if you’re prepared to push through the rough weeks, with a plan and some coffee.

Honestly, I barely passed Computer Networks in the middle of a brutal term, mostly because the assignment-heavy pace with frequent deadlines kept piling up and the platform quirks kept adding stress. Dr. Park is sharp, but the instructions left too much room for interpretation, and the forums were usually helpful yet a bit dismissive when I asked for clarifications. I’d compare it to a prerequisite that feels easier, and yeah, I’d not take it again, even though I did learn bits that might help in industry work

Calculus II with Dr. Singh felt doable but not friendly for my schedule. I mostly relied on recordings and notes because live lectures didn’t line up with my full‑time job, and the few in‑class demos didn’t always click. The group work helped when our team actually stayed coordinated, but if one person dropped the tempo, it slowed everyone down. The assessment mix seemed off compared to what we covered in lectures, and grading comments would show up days late, which made it hard to fix mistakes before the next item. It’s one of those courses where, if you already know the adjacent material, you’ll move through it faster, but for me the motivation wavered even when I had time to sit down. I wouldn’t take it again, even though I did pick up some useful ideas along the way.

I mostly got through Database Systems by carving out short evening sessions, and the peer chats in the forums and with the TA helped more than lectures; feels like it filled gaps faster than the prerequisite did, though the tooling glitches dragged deadlines hard.

Cyber Security Basics with Dr. Miller was solid enough for someone juggling a full-time job and short evening study bursts. The recorded lectures are handy, though they’re a bit dry, and the course fits best if you already know some adjacent material. I appreciated the mostly individual work pace—deadlines and a week-long project kept me honest, but platform quirks kept sneaking in and stressing me out more than needed. Overall, it met my expectations and the effort felt aligned with the B grade I ended up with

Overall, Cyber Security Basics felt solid and genuinely sparked my curiosity, and I’d recommend it to others who come in with that same spark. I kept up with nearly every lecture, and I made it my main focus that term, but the grading felt a bit fuzzy—the rubric never quite clicked for me, even after a couple of office hours. The course leaned mostly toward individual work, and while I did learn a lot, I didn’t feel as much peer-to-peer buzz as I expected; others helped each other more than staff did. A late-semester turning point, where a practical quiz exposed gaps in my note-taking, stuck with me and changed how I approached the final assignment, which mattered a lot despite the few big assessments. Prof. Haddad is thoughtful, but the flow of some topics didn’t always align with my expectations.

I’m in my last semester and juggling a few heavy courses, so Cyber Security Basics felt like a useful check-in with industry stuff, even though my attendance faded mid-semester as other deadlines piled up. The LMS and submission flow were smooth, which helped when I managed to stay on top of things, but the collaboration expectations were unclear and I often didn’t know who was supposed to do what. TAs were responsive and practical when I asked for quick pivots, and the course did build well on the prerequisites, but I didn’t always enjoy it as much as I expected—still, I ended up appreciating the practical angle more than the teaching moments. A late-semester turning point around a capstone-style exercise stood out, anchoring this memory even as I drifted in and out of engagement.

I came into Data Structures thinking it would be a solid backbone for industry work, and I’ll admit I learned a lot, even if the ride felt bumpy. The material kind of crept up on me, and I relied on office hours to rescue the course when the stack felt rough at first, especially since I’m new to the discipline and still learning the basics. The prerequisite stuff did line up with what we tackled, but the grading rubric stayed vague enough to make me second-guess what was actually being rewarded. One memorable moment was Week 7’s exam week, where I realized I remembered more from the practice sets than from the lectures, which was oddly encouraging and frustrating at once.

This term I treated Cyber Security Basics as my main focus, and it felt like a heavy ride in the middle of a brutal semester. The slides were serviceable but hardly memorable, and the workload felt okay while the assignments were oddly mismatched to what we actually covered in lectures. I started with a confusing early patch about threat models that stuck with me and colored the rest of the term, even as I pushed through with my coding background and tried to salvage a practical angle that never quite landed.

Taking Computer Networks as an advanced elective felt necessary for my degree, but with a full-time job and only sporadic motivation I found myself relying on a few late-night forum threads and the TA’s office hours more than I expected. The first week confusion about packet flows set a tone—once I got that, the rest clicked enough, though the grading was a grind: a handful of big assessments where one slip felt huge, and a few tooling hiccups that wrecked a couple of deadlines in weeks with already tight

Linear Algebra was solid enough to get me through, but I started out strong and then my attendance faded as the weeks dragged on. The slides are serviceable but not memorable, and I barely scraped by after a rough mid-semester crunch; the software stack felt rough at first but loosened up a bit later. I’m glad I stuck with it, though I’d have appreciated clearer communication on deadlines and more chance to collaborate.

Calculus II with Dr. Chen was a required grind: I started pretty engaged, but attendance faded as deadlines piled up. The LMS and submission flow stayed smooth, TA help was practical, but feedback arrived too late to matter. I’d only recommend with real prep.

I came into Calculus II trying to fit my schedule more than chasing excitement for the subject, and the course mostly delivered that steady, doable pace. Prof. Cohen explains things clearly in lectures with decent pacing, and the tooling for homework and practice problems is pretty user-friendly, which helped me stay afloat even when I fell behind and then had to scramble to catch up around deadlines. The forums are a mixed bag—some threads are genuinely helpful, others feel a bit dismissive when you post a basic question, which left me occasionally wishing for a quicker, more patient response. The grading rubric itself feels vague, and feedback sometimes shows up sparse until it’s almost too late to act on it, which pushed me to rely on memory of the last few problem sets rather than a steady guide. One memorable week was the midterm push, where the format and a few tricky quick questions kept me on my toes longer than I’d like. Overall, it’s mid-program core stuff with solid lecture delivery and decent tool support, but I wish the feedback timing and rubric were more transparent.

I stuck with nearly every lecture for this OS course because I needed it for my specialization, and I’m glad the recorded talks helped when I fell behind, even if they felt dry to sit through. The grading felt murky at times and I’m unsure whether my C reflected what I actually understood, since the assignments came in waves with frequent deadlines and some feedback was slow or inconsistent. What saved it for me was the exam structure: open-ended questions that leaned on proofs but still rewarded the ability to map ideas to real systems, which I could manage pretty well. A turning point late in the semester made me realize I did grasp core concepts, even if the day-to-day feedback didn’t always land, and I’m left weighing how much the late breakthroughs matter for the final grade.

I signed up for the Machine Learning course in my first semester because it’s supposed to be essential for the specialization, and I did feel like I was learning something practical even as the grind got real. The material felt okay to start—accessible enough at first, then it ramps up quickly, and I found myself scrambling to keep up during a mid-semester crunch when the deadlines started piling on. There were just a few assessments, but each one mattered a lot, so a single misstep could pull you down more than you’d expect; the grading rubric, though, felt vague and left me guessing what exactly counted as “adequate.” Dr. Park is thoughtful and careful in lectures, but I often walked away unsure whether I’d nailed the core concept or just followed the steps, which didn’t help when the email support was slow right around deadline time. A concrete moment sticks: the project where we had to tune a model with a limited parameter space; I remember finishing it at 2 a.m. and still not feeling confident about whether I’d generalized, even though the code ran. Overall, it’s useful enough to justify the effort, but I didn’t enjoy it as much as I expected.

I’d say the course is decent, but the pacing really wore me down while juggling a full-time job. Dr. Chen’s conceptual explanations helped, yet the thin real-life examples and late feedback left my rusty math self scrambling, especially before the big project deadlines.

Calculus II was a mixed ride while I balanced it with a couple of other demanding courses this last semester. The workload stayed doable in bursts, especially once I got the hang of the software stack and stopped fighting the rough edges of the tooling, though the prerequisite ramp-up felt sharp at first. I’m coming from a strong coding background but weaker on theory, so the slides were serviceable but not memorable, and I often wished for sooner feedback—by the time I finally saw notes, it felt a bit too late to adjust. I’m not sure I’d recommend it outright, but it did push me to tighten up problem-solving habits, and I did end up with an A after a curve.

Midway through the semester, Linear Algebra still feels like a slog and a puzzle at the same time. I picked it up mainly because I need it for a specialization, and the way Prof. Alvarez handles the proofs and matrices keeps nagging at the back of my brain in a good way, even when the tooling bites hard—tracking formulas in the learning platform during deadline weeks is rough and stalls progress. I’ve found the forums helpful sometimes, but often a bit dismissive, like if you’re stuck you should already know the answer, which isn’t great when you’re juggling a lot. A study group helps a lot; I don’t know what I’d do without someone to sanity-check a 3x3 invertible matrix before class, and the pace ramps up fast enough to feel like it’s catching you off guard. Overall, I learned a ton, but I’m not sure I’d recommend it to someone who isn’t committed to sticking with the

I signed up for Linear Algebra out of pure curiosity, but the workload and the way the grading rubric is explained left me frustrated yet still curious. I fell behind and caught up around deadlines, and the quick feedback helped me adjust, but the tooling problems during weeks with deadlines made everything feel messier than it should be. Prof. Rios is clearly capable, but the pace and the prerequisites feel like more is assumed than advertised, and the vibe was a bit thin in office hours once I finally asked about a matrix

This summer course gave me a sense it could be useful, but the pacing felt brutal and the deadlines stacked up so fast I barely kept up. Office hours helped—they felt like a lifeline when the lectures left me unsure, and I left with a clearer idea of a single project approach, even if I’m still not sure the overall grade reflects my understanding.

I signed up for Linear Algebra because I heard it was useful for industry work, and I came in with a strong coding background but not much theory, which made the math feel oddly distant at first. Dr. Miller is clearly sharp, but the course assumes more prior knowledge than advertised, so I spent extra time chasing down foundational bits while juggling two other demanding courses. The assessments are few but each matters a lot, and I felt the pressure to prove myself on a single tough problem set rather than a steady stream of smaller checks. Email support is slow when deadlines loom, and feedback often arrives too late to fix the next submission, which left me frustrated mid-semester before the tone of the class settled into a slower pace.

I took Computer Networks hoping it would sharpen my industry chops, since I’m comfy with proofs but not so confident with real system stuff, and Prof. Cohen kept saying it would be practical. The pacing starts accessible but then ramps up quickly, and by week four I realized the math-y parts aren’t the hard thing so much as the day-to-day tooling and deployment concepts, which felt a bit dry in recorded lectures. Most of the work is solo, which suits my style, but I kept wishing for more structured peer discussion because I’m not sure my grasp transfers to a real network project yet. Grading has quirky moments—the last two assignments felt like the feedback came late or was uneven in quality, and one rubric seemed to hinge on a small implementation detail I hadn’t expected. I remember a chat in office hours where someone asked about why a certain routing policy mattered and Prof. Cohen clarified it with a concrete example from a campus VPN, which stuck with me more than the lecture slides. Overall it’s not easy, and I’m not sure the grade reflected my understanding, but I did pick up a few practical touchpoints that seemed pretty useful for industry work.

Calculus II left me feeling rusty but kept me engaged enough to drag myself to nearly every lecture, though the motivation window flickered irregularly and deadlines piled up. The explanations were solid conceptually, but the real-world examples were thin, and it often felt like the prerequisites assumed more than what was actually taught. I appreciated classmates helping each other more than anything from staff, and the grading felt unclear at times, especially around the final that seemed to come with a few surprise twists.

I felt stuck early on because the materials felt clunky and not very helpful, but the hands-on parts helped my coding background push through; setup and weekly feedback were sparse until late, and I’m tired of uneven weeks, yet the course did fill some gaps I’d feared.
